title: Record-Breaking Discovery: Oldest, Most Distant Quasar Unveiled, Scientists Confirm 【CBS News】
body:
Scientists have identified the most distant quasar ever observed—a luminous beacon powered by a super‑massive black hole that began feeding on matter when the universe was less than a billion years old. Designated J1007+2115, the object lies at a redshift of z ≈ 7.5, placing it roughly 13 billion light‑years from Earth and making it the earliest known active galactic nucleus. Its discovery not only pushes the frontier of cosmic distance but also rewrites the timeline for the formation of massive black holes in the infant universe.

The quasar was uncovered by an international team using a combination of deep‑infrared imaging from the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT) and spectroscopic follow‑up with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii. The object's extreme redshift means that the light reaching us today was emitted when the cosmos was only about 700 million years old, a period often referred to as the “cosmic dawn.” At that epoch, the first generations of stars and galaxies were igniting, and the intergalactic medium was still transitioning from opaque to transparent. Finding a fully formed quasar at this stage challenges prevailing theories that predict a slower buildup of black‑hole mass.

What makes J1007+2115 especially intriguing is the estimated mass of its central black hole—approximately 1.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Such a colossal object would have had to grow at near‑Eddington accretion rates, or perhaps even exceed them, for a few hundred million years to reach that size so early. Traditional models, which rely on steady, radiatively efficient accretion onto stellar‑mass seeds, struggle to account for such rapid growth. Some researchers now favor alternative pathways, including the direct collapse of massive gas clouds into black‑hole seeds of 10⁴–10⁵ solar masses, or episodes of super‑Eddington feeding facilitated by dense, gas‑rich environments typical of early galaxies.

The discovery also carries implications for the reionization era, when ultraviolet photons from the first luminous objects stripped electrons from neutral hydrogen across the universe. Quasars, with their prodigious output of high‑energy radiation, are thought to be significant contributors to this process. However, the rarity of such bright quasars at high redshift suggests they alone could not have reionized the cosmos. By measuring the quasar’s spectral imprint on surrounding intergalactic gas, astronomers can refine estimates of the ionization state at that epoch, offering a new probe of how quickly the universe transitioned to transparency.

Beyond its scientific import, J1007+2115 underscores the power of next‑generation survey instruments. The object was initially flagged in data from the Wide‑field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) and the Dark Energy Survey (DES), both of which have demonstrated the ability to sift through billions of sources to isolate the faintest, most distant candidates. Looking ahead, the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are expected to dramatically expand the census of early quasars, potentially uncovering objects even closer to the Big Bang. Each new find will tighten constraints on black‑hole seed formation, accretion physics, and the timeline of cosmic reionization.

As astronomers continue to push the observational horizon, the existence of a massive, actively feeding black hole at such an early cosmic age serves as a reminder that the universe’s formative years were far more dynamic than once imagined. The record‑setting quasar not only rewrites the story of black‑hole growth but also opens fresh avenues for exploring the interplay between the first galaxies and the evolving intergalactic medium. With more powerful telescopes on the horizon, the next decade promises to reveal whether J1007+2115 is an outlier or the tip of an iceberg of ancient, luminous beacons waiting to be discovered.
